name: Motor Yachts
subtitle: Power, comfort, and effortless cruising
heroImageAlt: A motor yacht cruising near the coast
shortDescription: Flybridge and express motor yachts built for comfortable cruising, entertaining, and covering miles quickly.
longDescription:
Motor yachts are the most popular category of boat for sale, and for good reason: they combine speed, creature comforts, and low-maintenance operation into a single package. Most range from 40 to 90+ feet and are powered by twin diesel inboards, giving owners the range to cruise coastally or cross open water without the learning curve that comes with sail.

Inside, motor yachts typically prioritize living space over performance — full-beam salons, multiple staterooms, a flybridge for entertaining, and increasingly sophisticated electronics and stabilization systems that make them comfortable even in a chop. They're the natural choice for owners who want to host guests, entertain at the dock, or take extended trips without sacrificing air conditioning and hot showers.
whatToExpect: Twin diesel engines with cruising speeds of 20-30+ knots
Spacious salons, multiple staterooms, and full galleys
Flybridge or upper helm stations for entertaining underway
Bow and stern thrusters that make docking approachable for owner-operators
A broad range of builders from production (Sea Ray, Bayliner) to Italian luxury (Azimut, Ferretti, Sunseeker)
bestFor: Families who want space and comfort
Owners who plan to entertain at the dock or underway
First-time yacht owners who want easier handling than a sailboat
Coastal cruising and weekend getaways

name: Sailing Yachts
subtitle: Classic seamanship, wind-powered range, and quiet passages
heroImageAlt: A sailing yacht under full sail
shortDescription: Monohull cruisers designed for bluewater passages, coastal cruising, and the satisfaction of sailing under your own power.
longDescription:
Sailing yachts remain the boat of choice for owners who value seamanship, efficiency, and the ability to cover long distances without burning fuel. Production builders like Beneteau, Jeanneau, and Bavaria dominate the volume end of the market with comfortable, easy-to-handle cruisers, while brands like Oyster and Hallberg-Rassy build premium bluewater yachts meant for ocean crossings.

Modern sailing yachts have closed much of the comfort gap with motor yachts — think in-mast furling, electric winches, bow thrusters, and generously appointed interiors — while still rewarding owners with the lower operating costs and range that only sail can offer. They tend to have a shallower learning curve than people expect, especially with in-mast or in-boom furling systems that simplify sail handling for a shorthanded crew.
whatToExpect: Monohull designs from 30 to 60+ feet, most with a single mast (sloop rig)
Auxiliary diesel engines for maneuvering and calm-wind passages
Lower fuel costs and longer range than comparable motor yachts
A learning curve around sail trim, points of sail, and docking under wind
Strong resale and a large, active community of owners and clubs
bestFor: Owners who want to learn or practice traditional seamanship
Bluewater cruising and long-distance passages
Lower long-term fuel and operating costs
Sailors moving up from dinghies or club racing

name: Catamarans
subtitle: Stability, space, and shallow-draft freedom
heroImageAlt: A sailing catamaran anchored near a beach
shortDescription: Twin-hull sail and power boats known for their stability, wide-open living spaces, and popularity in the charter market.
longDescription:
Catamarans have grown from a niche category into one of the fastest-growing segments of the boat-for-sale market, driven largely by charter operators and owners who want the stability and space a twin-hull design provides. Because the hulls sit apart rather than heeling under sail, catamarans stay level at anchor and underway — a major draw for families, first-time owners, and anyone prone to seasickness.

Builders like Lagoon, Fountaine Pajot, and Leopard (built by Robertson & Caine) dominate the sailing catamaran market, while a growing number of power catamarans offer the same stability with the convenience of twin diesel engines and no sails to manage. The tradeoff for that stability and space is typically a higher purchase price and wider beam, which can limit marina and haul-out options.
whatToExpect: Wide, stable decks with minimal heeling under sail or power
Expansive interior volume relative to length — often more living space than a monohull of the same size
Shallow draft that opens up anchorages monohulls can't reach
Higher purchase price and wider beam that can limit slip availability
Strong charter market demand, which supports resale value
bestFor: Families and groups who prioritize stability and space
Owners considering putting the boat into charter
Shallow-water cruising in the Bahamas, Caribbean, or Gulf Coast
Anyone sensitive to the heel and motion of a monohull

name: Sport Fishers
subtitle: Built to chase fish offshore, then come home in comfort
heroImageAlt: A sport fishing yacht running offshore
shortDescription: Convertible sportfishing boats with deep-V hulls, tournament-ready cockpits, and enough range to reach the canyons and beyond.
longDescription:
Sport fishers are purpose-built for serious offshore anglers, combining a deep-V hull for rough-water handling with a spacious cockpit designed around fighting chairs, tackle centers, and outriggers. Legacy builders like Hatteras and Bertram helped define the category, and it remains one of the most tradition-rich corners of the boat-for-sale market.

Most sport fishers are "convertibles," meaning the below-deck accommodations rival a motor yacht's, so owners can fish hard during the day and sleep comfortably at night. Twin diesel inboards and generous fuel capacity give them the range to reach canyon edges and blue-water grounds, and a raised tower or flybridge improves the ability to spot fish from a distance.
whatToExpect: Deep-V hulls optimized for rough offshore water and following seas
Large cockpits with fighting chairs, transom doors, and tackle/bait centers
Towers or tuna towers for spotting fish and trolling visibility
Twin diesels with the range and fuel capacity to reach offshore canyons
Convertible layouts that combine fishing capability with cruising accommodations
bestFor: Serious offshore and tournament anglers
Owners who want a boat capable of both fishing and overnight cruising
Rough-water performance and following-sea handling
Buyers drawn to legacy American boatbuilding (Hatteras, Bertram, Viking)

name: Trawlers
subtitle: Slow, efficient, long-range passagemakers
heroImageAlt: A trawler yacht at anchor in a calm harbor
shortDescription: Full-displacement passagemakers built for efficient, long-range cruising rather than speed.
longDescription:
Trawlers trade speed for range and efficiency, running at 7-10 knot displacement speeds that sip fuel compared to a planing motor yacht. That efficiency, paired with heavy-displacement hulls and large fuel tanks, makes trawlers the boat of choice for owners planning extended cruises — up the coast, along the Great Loop, or across an ocean on a passagemaker like a Nordhavn.

The slower pace comes with real advantages: a smoother, more stable ride, lower running costs, and layouts built around comfortable long-term living rather than day-tripping. Builders like Grand Banks, Kadey-Krogen, and Nordhavn have each built loyal followings around this style of cruising, and used trawlers hold their value well thanks to steady demand from cruisers who know exactly what they want.
whatToExpect: Full-displacement hulls with cruising speeds around 7-10 knots
Excellent fuel efficiency and long range compared to planing hulls
Stable, comfortable motion in a seaway
Layouts optimized for extended liveaboard cruising
A dedicated resale market of experienced long-range cruisers
bestFor: Extended cruising and liveaboard trips (Great Loop, coastal, offshore passages)
Owners who prioritize fuel efficiency and range over speed
Retirees and full-time cruisers
Buyers who want a smoother ride in rough conditions

name: Mega Yachts
subtitle: Superyacht-scale luxury, crew, and range
heroImageAlt: A large mega yacht at anchor
shortDescription: Large-scale motor yachts, typically 80 feet and up, built with full crew quarters and superyacht-level systems and finish.
longDescription:
Mega yachts sit at the top of the market — generally 80 feet and longer, with the volume, range, and systems complexity that require a professional crew rather than an owner-operator. Builders like Azimut Grande, Ferretti, Sunseeker, and Benetti compete at this end with custom or semi-custom interiors, multiple decks, and amenities like beach clubs, tenders, and dedicated crew quarters.

Owning at this scale is a different proposition than a mid-size motor yacht: budgets typically include a captain and crew, dockage at facilities that can handle the draft and beam, and maintenance programs closer to commercial vessel standards. In exchange, owners get a genuinely different level of comfort, range, and entertaining space — the kind of yacht built to host, not just to cruise.
whatToExpect: Length generally starting around 80 feet and scaling to 150+ feet
Professional crew required for operation, navigation, and maintenance
Multiple decks, tender garages, and dedicated crew quarters
Significantly higher acquisition and annual operating costs
Custom or semi-custom interiors from major European builders
bestFor: Owners planning to run a crewed, full-service yacht
Large-scale entertaining and extended guest stays
Buyers considering a charter program to offset ownership costs
Long-range, multi-region cruising (Mediterranean, Caribbean, Bahamas)

name: Express Cruisers
subtitle: Sporty, single-level cruising for day trips and weekends
heroImageAlt: An express cruiser running at speed
shortDescription: Compact, single-deck cruisers built for fast day trips, weekending, and easy trailering or slip storage.
longDescription:
Express cruisers fill the space between a bowrider and a full flybridge motor yacht — a single-level cabin design, planing hull, and enough speed to make quick work of a day on the water. They typically range from the low 20s up to about 45 feet, with a small cabin below offering a berth, head, and galley for overnighting without the size or cost of a larger yacht.

Because they're simpler to operate and maintain than a flybridge yacht, express cruisers are a popular entry point for boaters moving up from a runabout, and a popular second boat for owners who want something quick and low-maintenance for weekend trips. Builders like Sea Ray, Formula, and Chaparral are well represented in this category.
whatToExpect: Single-level layout with a small cabin below for overnighting
Planing hulls with strong performance and fuel-efficient cruising speeds
Lower purchase price and easier maintenance than flybridge motor yachts
Good fit for trailering or standard-size slips
Popular as a step-up boat or a simpler second yacht
bestFor: Day trips, watersports, and weekend getaways
Owners moving up from a smaller runabout or bowrider
Buyers who want performance without a large crew or budget
Coastal and inland lake cruising

name: Center Consoles
subtitle: Open-deck versatility for fishing, diving, and days on the water
heroImageAlt: A center console boat running offshore
shortDescription: Open, walk-around boats built around a center helm — the most versatile platform for fishing, diving, and casual day boating.
longDescription:
The center console is the do-everything boat of the modern market: an open deck wrapped around 360 degrees of the helm, room to fish from any angle, and enough beam and horsepower on the bigger models to handle real offshore conditions. Builders like Boston Whaler, Regulator, and Everglades have pushed the category well past its inshore-skiff roots into 40+ foot offshore boats with triple or quadruple outboards.

Because there's no fixed cabin structure to work around, center consoles are prized for their versatility — rig one for tournament fishing, another for diving and watersports, another as a fast, comfortable family day boat. Smaller models trailer easily and store cheaply; larger ones compete directly with sport fishers for serious offshore capability.
whatToExpect: Open, unobstructed deck space usable from every angle
Outboard power, often twin, triple, or quadruple engines on larger models
Strong resale value and a very active used market
Easy trailering and storage on smaller (20-30ft) models
Larger models (35ft+) capable of serious offshore fishing and cruising
bestFor: Inshore and offshore fishing
Diving, watersports, and casual family day trips
Owners who want one boat that can do several jobs well
Buyers who prioritize easy trailering or simple storage

name: Sloops
subtitle: The classic single-masted rig for cruising and racing alike
shortDescription: Single-masted sailboats with a mainsail and single headsail — the simplest, most common rig in modern sailing.
longDescription:
The sloop rig — one mast, a mainsail, and a single headsail — is the most common configuration in modern sailboats, and for good reason: it's efficient upwind, straightforward to trim, and easier to handle shorthanded than rigs with more sails to manage. Most production sailing yachts you'll find for sale, from compact daysailers to 40-foot cruisers, use some variation of the sloop rig.

Within the category there's a wide range, from lighter, race-oriented sloops like the Beneteau First series to heavier, cruising-focused designs meant for long passages. Because the rig is so widely used, parts, rigging knowledge, and sailmakers are easy to find, which keeps ownership costs and complexity lower than more specialized rigs like a ketch or schooner.
whatToExpect: Single mast with mainsail and one headsail (jib or genoa)
The most common and best-understood rig — easy to find parts, rigging support, and sailmakers
Efficient upwind performance compared to multi-masted rigs
Sizes ranging from small daysailers to 40+ foot cruisers and racers
A large used market with strong parts and community support
bestFor: New sailors learning fundamentals on a simple, well-understood rig
Club racing and one-design competition
Coastal and weekend cruising
Owners who want easy access to parts, rigging, and local sailing knowledge
